summary: Defines algorithm implementation requirements and usage guidance for DNSSEC, to make sure there is at least one algorithm that all implementations support. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 9904.

eli5.summary: DNS security uses different math recipes. This says which ones to support so everyone can understand each other.

questions: is rsasha1 still allowed in dnssec
what is the recommended dnssec algorithm
subtitle: Which signing and digest algorithms DNSSEC software must, should or must not support.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC can use many cryptographic algorithms, and resolvers and servers only interoperate if there is at least one algorithm every implementation supports. Algorithms also age and weaken over time.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists each DNSKEY algorithm and each DS/CDS digest algorithm with separate requirement levels for signing (or delegation) and for validation, and explains the reasoning. It expects changes to come gradually, in later updates.
tldr.outcome: ECDSAP256SHA256 became the recommended algorithm for new deployments and SHA-256 the recommended DS digest. This RFC has since been obsoleted by RFC 9904 and updated by RFC 9157.

today: RFC 8624 has been obsoleted by RFC 9904 and updated by RFC 9157, so those are the places to look for current guidance. It is itself the replacement for RFC 6944.

sections.title: Why the Requirements Need Updating
sections.content:
DNSSEC authenticates DNS data using signing algorithms defined in several RFCs. To keep resolvers and authoritative servers interoperable, a set of mandatory-to-implement algorithms is defined. RFC 8624 replaces the earlier list in RFC 6944.

Cryptography keeps moving: new algorithms appear, old ones turn out weaker than thought, and attacks get cheaper as computing power grows. So the requirements have to be revisited from time to time, and the choices are meant to be conservative.
sections.eli5: Locks get picked and new locks get invented. So the club has to keep re-checking which locks are still safe.

sections.title: How Requirement Levels Change
sections.content:
The RFC uses RECOMMENDED and NOT RECOMMENDED in place of SHOULD and SHOULD NOT because it expresses the intent more clearly to implementers. An algorithm is listed as MAY only when it has been downgraded from MUST or RECOMMENDED. Algorithms in the IANA registries that are not mentioned MAY be implemented.

Deprecation is meant to be gradual. Unless there are strong security reasons, an algorithm goes from MUST to NOT RECOMMENDED or MAY rather than straight to MUST NOT, and a new algorithm is introduced as RECOMMENDED rather than MUST. An unknown DNSKEY algorithm makes a zone look insecure, so algorithms at NOT RECOMMENDED or lower should not be used to create new DNSKEYs. Once use is low enough, an algorithm can become MUST NOT so that recursive resolvers can drop validation support. Recursive nameservers are encouraged to keep support for everything not marked MUST NOT.
sections.eli5: When a handshake gets old, the club does not ban it overnight. It first says "please stop teaching it" and only later says "never use it", so nobody gets locked out.

sections.title: DNSKEY Signing Algorithms
sections.content:
The core of the RFC is a table of DNSKEY algorithms with one level for DNSSEC signing and one for DNSSEC validation. RSAMD5 (1), DSA (3) and DSA-NSEC3-SHA1 (6) are MUST NOT for both. RSASHA1 (5), RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 (7) and RSASHA512 (10) are NOT RECOMMENDED for signing but MUST be validated, because they are still deployed. RSASHA256 (8) and ECDSAP256SHA256 (13) are MUST for both.

ECDSAP384SHA384 (14) and ED448 (16) are MAY for signing and RECOMMENDED for validation. ED25519 (15) is RECOMMENDED for both, and the RFC expects it to become the future default once validators support it widely enough. ECC-GOST (12) is MUST NOT for signing and MAY for validation.

The RFC gives reasons: MD5 is being deprecated across the industry, DSA is vulnerable to private key compromise if the random number generator is weak, and ECDSAP256SHA256 gives more strength with a shorter signature than RSA, which means smaller DNS packets. EdDSA does not need a unique random number per signature and resists side-channel attacks better. It is RECOMMENDED to use the deterministic ECDSA procedure from RFC 6979. The headline advice is that new deployments should use ECDSAP256SHA256, and RSA users should upgrade to it.
sections.eli5: There is a list of secret-handshake styles. A few are banned, some old ones are still understood but should not be taught, and one modern one is the favorite for newcomers.

sections.title: DS and CDS Digest Algorithms
sections.content:
A second table covers the digest algorithms used in Delegation Signer (DS) records, and the same levels apply to the Child DS (CDS) record type from RFC 7344. SHA-256 (2) is MUST for both delegation and validation. SHA-1 (1) is MUST NOT for creating new DS and CDS records, but validators MUST still implement it because it is widely used. GOST R 34.11-94 (3) is MUST NOT for delegation and MAY for validation. SHA-384 (4) is MAY for delegation and RECOMMENDED for validation.

Digest algorithm 0 (NULL) is a special case that appears only in CDS records, where it signals removal of the DS at the parent as described in RFC 8078. The operational recommendation for new and existing deployments is that SHA-256 is the RECOMMENDED DS and CDS algorithm.
sections.eli5: The same idea applies to the fingerprint a parent keeps of a child's key. One fingerprint recipe is the favorite and the oldest one must not be used for new fingerprints.

sections.title: Security and Operational Cautions
sections.content:
The algorithms marked MUST or RECOMMENDED are not known to be broken in the cryptographic sense, and research suggests they will stay secure for the foreseeable future, though not necessarily forever. The RFC warns that retiring an algorithm too soon would downgrade a zone signed with it to the equivalent of an unsigned zone, so deprecation must be slow and based on measurement of use.

Algorithm rollovers in a live zone are complex; see RFC 6781 and RFC 7583. Upgrading the DS algorithm at the same time as rolling a new Key Signing Key leads to validation failures, so administrators MUST finish the DS algorithm upgrade before starting a KSK rollover. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: If the club forgets an old handshake too early, members who still use it get treated as strangers. So changes must be slow, and you should not change two things at once.
